title: Valid Anagram
directAnswer: Two strings are anagrams iff they have identical character counts. Fast-fail on differing lengths, then count characters of one string and decrement with the other — if every count returns to zero, it's an anagram. O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. Sorting both strings and comparing is the simpler O(n log n) fallback.

rules: **Length check first** — different lengths can never be anagrams, and it's a free O(1) exit.
Increment for `s`, decrement for `t` over **one** map — cleaner than building two maps and comparing.
A fixed 26-slot array beats a hash map for lowercase English — `O(1)` space and faster constants.
For Unicode / arbitrary characters, use a hash map keyed by the code point, not a 26-array.
Sorting both strings is the easy answer to fall back on, but say it's `O(n log n)` vs the `O(n)` counter.
whenToUse: Compare two strings for identical multiset of characters
Detect rearrangements / permutations of a word
antiSignals: Need to group many anagrams together → sort-key the words (Group Anagrams)
Order matters, not just multiset → direct equality or sequence comparison
Streaming / sliding comparison → fixed-window frequency (Permutation in String)
remember.takeaway: Anagram = equal character histograms. The counting array is the building block for Group Anagrams, Permutation in String, and Minimum Window Substring — all of which compare frequency maps.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model 'anagram' as a frequency-count equality and pick a fixed array over a hash map when the alphabet is small.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Skipping the length check, or assuming ASCII when the interviewer slips in 'what about Unicode?'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use a single counter (increment then decrement), state the O(1)-space claim depends on a bounded alphabet, and pivot cleanly to a hash map for Unicode.

problemStatement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise.

An **anagram** is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, using all the original letters exactly once.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters
Follow-up: what if the inputs contain Unicode characters?
understanding: Decide whether `t` is just `s` with its letters shuffled. That's true exactly when both strings contain the same letters with the same multiplicities — i.e. identical character frequency tables.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the comparison case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per constraints, both are lowercase, so yes treat them as-is. If mixed case, normalize first or count case separately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear — just a–z, or Unicode?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Constraints say lowercase English (26 letters), so a fixed array works. The follow-up asks about Unicode, where a hash map is required.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do whitespace and punctuation count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not in this version. If they did, you'd decide whether to strip them before counting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the strings differ in length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and if they do the answer is immediately false — that's the first check.

examples.explanation: Both have a×3, n×1, g×1, r×1, m×1.
s has a 't', t has a 'c' — frequencies differ.
Different lengths can never be anagrams.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Counting wins on time; sorting wins on simplicity. Alphabet size decides array vs map.

approaches.name: Sort Both Strings
approaches.whenToMention: The simplest correct answer — good to state first, then offer the linear counter.
hints: If two strings are anagrams, what happens when you sort each of them?
Sort the characters of both strings and compare the results for equality.
It's correct and tiny, but sorting costs O(n log n) — beatable with counting.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting dominates at O(n log n); the comparison is O(n). Space is O(n) for the sorted copies (Java char arrays / Python lists).
approaches.explanation:
Anagrams become identical once their letters are sorted into canonical order. So sort `s`, sort `t`, and check the two sorted forms are equal. A length mismatch makes them unequal automatically, but checking length first is a cheaper early exit.

**Why it works.** Sorting maps every permutation of the same multiset to the same string. Two strings share that canonical form exactly when they're anagrams. It's the easiest solution to get right under pressure.
approaches.insight: Sorting is the universal 'canonicalize then compare' trick — the same idea keys Group Anagrams. The downside is the log factor; counting removes it.

dryRun.intro: Sort each string and compare character by character.

java.explanation: Different lengths can't be anagrams — cheap early exit.
Sorted forms are equal iff the originals are anagrams.

python.explanation: Free fast-fail before doing any sorting work.
sorted() returns the canonical letter order; equal lists ⇒ anagram.

pitfalls: Skipping the length check and relying only on equality (still correct, just slightly slower to fail).
Forgetting sorting allocates O(n) extra space.

approaches.name: Frequency Count — One Counter (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'increment for s, decrement for t, expect all zeros'.
hints: Anagrams have identical letter counts. How could you compare counts without sorting?
Build a frequency table from s, then subtract t's letters from it.
If any count goes negative (or isn't zero at the end), they aren't anagrams. With 26 letters the table is a fixed-size array → O(1) space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes over the strings and one over the 26-slot table = O(n). The table size is bounded by the alphabet, so space is O(1) for lowercase English.
approaches.explanation:
After the length check, walk `s` incrementing a count per character, then walk `t` decrementing the same counts. If `t` is an anagram, every increment is matched by a decrement and all counts end at zero. For a 26-letter alphabet, the counter is a fixed `int[26]` indexed by `c - 'a'` — constant space and great cache behavior.

**Why one counter, not two.** Building two maps and comparing them works but doubles the memory and adds a comparison pass. Incrementing then decrementing in a single table collapses the comparison into 'is everything zero?'. You can even bail early inside the second loop the moment a count dips below zero.
approaches.insight: A frequency array is a histogram of the string. Anagram-ness is just histogram equality, and subtracting one histogram from another and checking for all-zero is the cleanest way to assert that. This exact histogram-compare powers Permutation in String and Find All Anagrams.

dryRun.intro: Increment over s, decrement over t. All counts should return to zero.

java.explanation: Unequal lengths short-circuit before allocating the counter.
'a'-offset maps a..z to 0..25; increment for s.
Decrement for t in the SAME pass — net zero means balanced.
Any non-zero slot means the letter counts didn't match.

python.explanation: Fixed 26-slot histogram → O(1) space for lowercase English.

python.line: return all(c == 0 for c in count)
python.explanation: Every slot back to zero ⇒ identical histograms ⇒ anagram.

diagrams.title: Counter after each operation
diagrams.caption: Increment for s, decrement for t. Ends all-zero for an anagram.

edgeCases.behavior: Equal length 0, no characters to count, all-zero table → true (empty strings are anagrams).
Switch the int[26] to a HashMap<Character,Integer> keyed by code point; the increment/decrement logic is unchanged.

pitfalls: Using int[26] for Unicode — index out of bounds or wrong results; use a map.
Forgetting the length check, then the counter can falsely balance for prefixes.
Comparing two separate maps instead of one signed counter — works but more code and memory.

commonMistakes: Not checking lengths first — wastes work and can mask mismatches.
Assuming ASCII / 26 letters when the follow-up introduces Unicode.
Building two frequency maps and comparing instead of one increment/decrement counter.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Hardcoding the 26-letter alphabet for Unicode
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An int[26] indexed by c - 'a' breaks the moment a character falls outside a–z (negative index or overflow). For arbitrary characters, key a hash map by the character itself.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int[] count = new int[26];
count[c - 'a']++; // crashes / wrong for non a-z
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
Map<Character, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
count.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Truthiness check that misses zero counts
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In Python, checking `if count.get(c)` treats a legitimately-zero count as falsy. Always compare counts explicitly or verify all values equal zero.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return not any(count.values())  # ok, but reads as 'no truthy', confusing
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return all(v == 0 for v in count.values())

patternNote: Character-frequency comparison. Reach for it whenever two strings must match as multisets of characters. The counting table is the seed of Group Anagrams, Permutation in String, and the sliding-window anagram problems.
